title: Can I find wifey on Substack?
subtitle: Half joking. Half dead serious.
html:
Modern dating: the deadest of dead horses. I wish not to beat it, but to give it a gentle tap, and garnish it with a dusting of (heterosexual) male perspective—which will, admittedly, be outside the norm for most men—and then propose a rather peculiar workaround for the ails of Hinge Life ™️ and manifest delusion. I’ve touched on my dating experiences here briefly, so I won’t belabor the point. Again, dead horse. But my two-pronged TLDR is that a) there are, indeed, widespread social pathologies that make many—and, perhaps, most—people undateable, and b) the problem of finding a high-quality partner—difficult, but tractable—is nearly unsolvable through dating apps.

Much to my amusement, and, of course, my chagrin, the failures of Hinge Life ™️ map seamlessly onto those of the hiring process—both are matching problems, fit versus unfit, and I’ve been kicked in the nuts by both. Recruiters (women) are flooded with a torrent of indistinguishable applicants (men), many reasonably fit for the role, as well as tides of incompetent incels whose applications are both bewildering and disturbing. Anxiety and overwhelm churn as the pool fills faster than it can be distilled, analyzed, and emptied. While recruiters leverage automated systems to purge the pool of unfit applicants, women on dating apps don’t have that luxury. So women, understandably, are prone to withdraw—neglecting and ghosting hopeful suitors waiting in the queue, not out of malice, but out of self-preservation.

Men, often unaware of the dynamics at play, risk drawing incorrect—even destructive—conclusions about themselves and their female counterparts. As with applying for jobs, the deafening silence heard when sending likes can be interpreted as a personal failure to offer value, and evidence that women, cruel and unrelenting in their judgements, find us wanting.

While this interpretation may contain kernels of truth—for many a man should indeed be found wanting—obscurity, rather than insufficiency, is more the culprit of isolation. If a man cannot be distinguished from the sea of competitors in any meaningful way, a woman cannot justify choosing him. After all, she wants him to be special. She wants him to be hers.

But how can a man cast himself apart from the rest when all he is given to do so is a half-dozen pictures and a few hundred characters? Does he need to strike the perfect balance of wit and lightheartedness? Humor and competence? Does he have to angle the camera just so, revealing a tasteful amount of bicep, but not so much as to seem conceited? Should he mention his hobbies? His passions? Will he seem desperate if his replies are thoughtful and earnest? Will he seem arrogant and careless if they’re not? But how can he expect women to read all those words? They probably don’t care about what he has to say anyway—just about how he looks. But if he finds the lighting and angles that look the best, does that make him a douchebag? A fuckboy? But if he doesn’t, is he a slouch? Is there any real set of winning conditions? No. He will remain obscure.

I know this from experience. Hinge stores likes in a queue. FIFO. First-In-First-Out. So if you’re not first, you’re buried, crushed under the weight of dozens of other profiles that, at first glance, look remarkably similar to yours. As a man, it’s not uncommon for your profile to never even get seen, and, if it does, it’s likely the woman’s journey from the top of the stack to your gym mirror pic created such disgust and apathy that she won’t give you more than a second of consideration unless you are a certified Chad. This is because Chads are rare and therefore distinguishable from the herd.

The FIFO problem became clear to me when I tested HingeX, the paid version, where your likes get put on the top of the stack—first in. Both quality and quantity of my matches increased by an order of magnitude. The problem was clear, and, to my relief and dismay, it was not me, nor was it the women. We, as men, are not battling women or their standards so much as a broken app design and an inability to provide meaningful context. Provide enough context, and you can be made singular. And once you become 1 of 1, you stand a chance of being chosen.

The friends-to-lovers arc is the pinnacle example of context’s power. Two people, once strangers, growing ever closer, carefully assembling mental models of one another, filling in gaps with each shared moment until, at last, they can no longer ignore the beauty of their geometric alignment—edges supporting edges; vertices interlocked; structurally sound.

Alternatively, a toned-down friends-to-lovers arc can happen in third spaces. Gyms, cafes, and run clubs all allow for frequent touchpoints for regulars. In such settings, if we’re brave, we can shed the awkwardness of remaining strangers with people whose faces we know well, letting them begin weaving neural tapestries of who we are. With each interaction, they spin a thread, and the context grows. With time, we make ourselves known to each other, and, with time, we make ourselves unique. Once known—once singular—we are well-positioned to ask, “Coffee?”

These paths to partnership—while effective—have major shortcomings. The friends-to-lovers arc presupposes an attractive female friend, which isn’t always common for the non-Chad. The third spaces, on the other hand, cost time and energy that a focused, forward-charging man might be unwilling to pay at critical periods in his life. Personally, satisfying my current desire for job security, intellectual growth, and creation demands my full attention. Thus, while the in-person kindling of flames—the creation of context—is millennia old and undeniably human, it remains, for now, highly undesirable.

How, then, do I make myself known? How, then, can I cast myself into strangers’ minds so they may one day come to know me from a distance?

Perhaps the answer lay here—beneath my callused fingertips, strewn across the page, my words chasing the blinking cursor. What better way to spin silks of Charlie in others’ minds than to spin them here, weaving my world and sewing myself singular. Through creation and vulnerability, I can lay tripwires so that if a woman—curious and brave—ever trips over my thread and finds herself intrigued, she can follow it to its origin. Step by step, word by word, her fingers traverse the thread, and a fuzzy image of Me—my inner world—emerges from obscurity and into focus.

While outlandish—and, perhaps, slightly arrogant—this strategy immediately presents two major challenges. I have never written a viral Substack post, and I currently (October 2026) have 26 subscribers. Neither fact precludes my posts from going viral and reaching wifey, but they do make the odds vanishingly small. Thus, I must claw my way out of the cold darkness of Substack invisibility and into the warm light of viewership. I must keep writing. More, better writing—writing that connects—will, in time, attract a critical mass. With a balance of earnestness and virality, my words might find the right woman and compel her to engage—climbing along my web of words—establishing a wider context than anyone ever could through dating apps or stilted cafe cold approaches.

Once context is established and curiosity piqued, once my thoughts and feelings, too raw to sensibly release into the wild, coalesce into an incomplete but digestible representation of Me, she will then reach out. Out of the darkness and into the DMs. At last, first contact. She will remark on what a strange collage I am, and how I’m “not like other men.” To which I will respond in the only way I know how, calling forth all my years of life—the memories of isolation, judgement, and misalignment—to the surface between inner and outer worlds—but kept just below it—letting only a shard, dulled with humor, emerge from the emotional waters and into the open air. “Oh…*dramatic pause* I know, dear,” I’ll say. Then, with rapport built and her fragmented, yet meaningful, mental model of Charlie in place, she will ask, “Coffee?"

I’ll oblige, of course. After all, this was the plan all along. The date will be going as well as any could until wifey, clutching both hands around her mug, tilts her head to the side and says, “Ya know… I found that old post of yours about finding wifey on Substack.”

Uh oh.

“Don’t you find it a bit… ummm… egotistical to think that you could just write your way into having a bunch of girls in your DMs?”

I look at her, wide-eyed, now holding both my mug and my breath. I say nothing, desperately hoping she fills the space.

“But I have to say, I admire the divergent thinking.”

*Exhales*

My courage to speak returns.

“Well, I never wrote to have a bunch of girls in my DMs.”

She raises her eyebrows as if to call BS.

“Just one,” I say. “Just you, perhaps.”

“So you’re telling me you spent hours and days and years writing blog posts and building an audience just so I would message you first?” she asks.

I nod, thoroughly pleased with myself.

“You did all that… for a girl?”

With softening eyes and a wistful smile, I ask, “Isn’t that kind of the point?”

“What do you mean?” Her eyebrows now heavy and drawn together.

“Well…” I cut myself off, searching for words that wouldn’t make me sound like a complete lunatic—a common practice of mine.

“Well,” I start again, believing—however falsely—I had found a path through the minefield.

“I learned that almost any desirable outcome can be achieved by putting so much effort towards it that it would be unreasonable for it not to happen. If the desired outcome is skill development, I just need to put in hours of practice. It’d be unreasonable for me to suck at something I’ve spent 10,000 hours practicing. But if the desired outcome is locking in a super awesome, high-value woman, I need to become worthy of her. And THAT is what this is all for… kinda. It’s not necessarily FOR her, but it’s a means of becoming—becoming the kind of person for whom it’d be unreasonable to never find a high-value partner. Ya know? Like… I fully intend to become a high-value man—creating, contributing, protecting, providing, yada yada yada. So why wouldn’t I just Field of Dreams my way to wifey, ya know? ‘If you build it, they will come’ kind of vibe. But in this case, it’s ‘If Char builds Char, wifey will come.’ Does that make sense?”

“You’re insane,” she says.

I smile.

“Oh… I know, dear.”
